title: Developing Teaching: What YOU Do Matters Less Than What EVERYONE ELSE Does hat-everyone-else-does/
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Matthew Evans argues that a teacher's practice cannot be evaluated in isolation because its effects are always shaped by the interdependent behaviour of every other teacher in the school. Using an extended example of a teacher introducing mini-whiteboards, first alone and then as a whole-school initiative, he shows how the same pedagogical idea produces different outcomes depending on whether it's implemented in isolation or in concert, and how good intentions can still unravel through inconsistent expectations across colleagues, forgotten equipment, and drifting routines. He argues this interdependence is largely invisible and generates feedback loops too complex to predict in advance, meaning school leaders can only observe and respond rather than fully plan for outcomes. Evans notes the effect is more pronounced in secondary schools, where students cycle through many teachers a day, than in primary, though primary carries its own complicating factors. He closes with three practical implications: don't attribute a teacher's outcomes solely to their individual skill, factor interdependence explicitly into plans for developing teaching practice, and treat pedagogical innovation as something that must be allowed to emerge adaptively rather than simply be implemented top-down.
points: Evans's extended mini-whiteboard example shows the same technique succeeding when introduced school-wide but degrading over weeks as inconsistent routines and missing equipment creep in.
He argues explicitly against attributing a teacher's outcomes to individual skill alone, since the observable effect of any technique is 'contaminated' by every other teacher's practice.
He notes secondary schools face a more complex version of this interdependence than primary schools, simply because students pass through more teachers per day.
His practical takeaway is that pedagogical innovation 'cannot be implemented; it must be allowed to emerge,' arguing for adaptive rather than top-down rollout of new practices.
quotes: When it comes to developing your teaching practice, what you do matters somewhat less than what everyone else does. Such is the interdependence of teachers in a school.
It matters because many of our attempts to help teachers improve ignores this interdependence and assumes that the impact of a teacher’s pedagogy is predominantly due to their skill as a teacher.
Even as the lone innovator, the impact of the teacher’s actions are affected by the behaviour of other teachers in the school, even though their practice may not have changed.
Whatever an individual teacher does, the effect will be contaminated by other teachers’ practice.
The interdependencies are largely invisible and the feedback loops are multiple, which means it isn’t possible to predict how this is going to go. We can only observe and respond.
First, we should caution attributing the effect of a teacher’s actions entirely to the teacher’s skill.
Pedagogical innovation cannot be implemented; it must be allowed to emerge.
